# System Designer

A free browser game for learning system design. Practise 82 problems across 15 industries, study 41 lessons and see how your architecture handles spikes, outages and retries.

## Full guides

# Build the system. Survive the day. See why it held.

By System Designer
https://systemdesigner.io/guides/introducing-system-designer/

Meet System Designer: a free browser game with 82 system design problems, 41 lessons and a traffic day that puts your decisions to work.

A box labelled cache is easy to draw. Knowing what happens when that cache empties at lunchtime is harder. System Designer turns that gap into something you can play.

Build a real architecture, press Start and fast-forward through a whole day of traffic. A link goes viral. A building loses power. A provider asks you to slow down. Every request flows through your design as moving light, so you can see where the work goes and where it gets stuck.

Start with a small system

You do not need to know what a load balancer is. Your first system starts with a phone, a server and a database. When more people arrive, you add capacity, spread requests and remember repeated answers. The parts have a job before they have a name to memorise.

If you already build software, try the URL shortener. It sounds small: save a long address, return a short one, look it up later. Then ask how the same link behaves when a crowd taps it together. Read the constraints, make your estimate and see whether your explanation survives a day.

The habit is the game

Clarify the promise. Ask what can wait, what must be fresh and what may never be lost.

Do the numbers. Turn the audience into requests, stored bytes and work at the busiest step.

Draw a design. Connect parts and tune the capacity and policies you can explain.

Run the traffic day. Watch spikes, outages, waiting work and recovery.

Read the debrief. Compare reliability, speed, data safety and monthly cost, then change one thing.

The debrief is written in plain words. It tells you which event hurt, where requests failed and what the design cost. Hints and editorials help you investigate. A traffic score is evidence about this workload, while the correctness checks ask you to reason about duplicates, crashes and ordering that a moving dot cannot prove.

More than one way to practise

There are 41 lessons and 82 problems across 15 industries. Lessons focus on one mechanism. Problems put several mechanisms together, from small services to systems where an outage, an unfair customer or a late queue changes the answer.

Try Notification service when you want to separate accepting work from finishing it. Try One-to-one chat when bad connections and repeated messages matter. Use How to lead a design interview before a timed attempt. Interview mode on Medium and Hard problems asks you to lead the discussion and defend choices with evidence.

The daily challenge gives everyone the same seeded scenario for a date. A beat my design link carries the architecture with it, so a friend can replay it and compete. Sandbox leaves the score behind and lets you try a traffic pattern or event just to understand it.

Free, with no account needed

Play in the browser. There is no download, no subscription and no sign-up wall. Your progress stays on this device in the browser.

Optional Google or GitHub sign-in keeps progress across devices and adds challenge leaderboards. You can keep playing without it.

Prices, capacities and timings are rounded teaching approximations. A simulation cannot certify a production system, but it can make a useful question concrete: what did this choice protect, what did it cost, and what would make you change it?

Start with Your first system, then build the URL shortener. Predict the first bottleneck before you press Start.

# How to practise system design

By System Designer
https://systemdesigner.io/guides/how-to-practise-system-design/

A practical loop for turning a diagram into a design you can explain: clarify, estimate, predict a failure, test it and revise one decision.

A whiteboard helps you organise an explanation. It does not tell you whether the workers can drain the queue, whether the database becomes the bottleneck after a cache miss, or whether a retry repeats a charge. A convincing diagram can hide all three.

Practise the reasoning between the boxes. For each part, say which user promise it serves, which new failure it introduces and which measurement would make you remove it. That gives you something to test, rather than a picture to memorise.

Write the user promise first

Take Notification service. Is success accepting a message, reaching a provider or reaching a phone? Those are different boundaries. The scenario measures provider acceptance and has a separate waiting deadline. Copy the actual promise into your notes before choosing a queue.

Ask who uses the system, which operation matters most, whether data changes and what a failure may lose. Keep assumptions visible. If a missing answer could reverse a decision, state both possibilities and ask about that one first.

Estimate the work that reaches each step

Use Numbers you can do in your head to turn a peak rate and request mix into a per-path load. A total request rate does not mean every request reaches the database. A cache removes repeated reads; a retry adds work; fanout turns one action into many writes.

Keep average, normal peak and event peak in separate rows. Size for the relevant peak with room for recovery. Then ask whether that room is already committed to a failed zone. Do not promise the same spare capacity twice.

Use a repeatable practice loop

Read the brief and answer the clarification questions without drawing.

Estimate the busiest request path and state the units of every number.

Build the simplest connected design that could keep the promises.

Write a prediction: name the first limiting part and the event that exposes it.

Run the whole day. Record the measured failure, its time and the affected request type.

Change one decision, predict its effect and run again.

Explain the improvement and its cost. Then test a different situation before calling the idea learned.

Make one useful experiment

Suppose requests fail after a spike. One explanation is too little server capacity. Another is repeated misses reaching the database. Adding servers and a cache at once cannot distinguish them. Change just the suspected boundary, keep the workload fixed and compare database load as well as success rate.

The URL shortener is a useful first experiment because links do not change and reads dominate. Predict what happens when its cache empties, then compare your run with that prediction. Play this problem.

Keep correctness separate from throughput

A high score does not prove that a database transaction and an external payment happen atomically. Trace one logical operation through a lost reply and a crash. Where is its stable identity stored? When can a retry learn the result? What if the provider accepted work before your process stopped?

Use Exactly once, on purpose and the problem’s checked traces to practise that explanation. State what the traffic run measured and what still needs a protocol argument. Both matter in a design discussion.

Finish with a decision you can defend

Keep a short record: the promise, your estimate, the first failure, your change and the result. Include an alternative you rejected and the condition under which it becomes better. On the next attempt, begin from the brief again rather than copying the finished diagram.

When ordinary Practice feels comfortable, use Interview mode on a Medium or Hard problem. Speak through clarification and estimates before building. Defend a choice using the run’s evidence and a tested claim. The goal is a clear chain from requirement to decision to observed result, not a perfect drawing.

# A two-week system design interview plan

By System Designer
https://systemdesigner.io/guides/two-week-system-design-plan/

Fourteen days of lessons, traffic experiments and design explanations, with Interview mode in the second week. Every task links to a real lesson or problem.

Use this as a sequence of focused sessions, not a promise of interview success. If a mechanism still feels like a name on a box, repeat that day before moving on. Keep a notebook of predictions and results so progress means better decisions rather than more finished pages.

How to use each session

Read the linked lessons, try the named problem and write a short explanation afterwards. During the first week, use Practice to investigate failures. During the second week, use Interview mode on Medium and Hard problems before reading hints or reference designs. Its clock guides the session; the exercise is to lead the reasoning and test your claims.

Day 1: Start with one request

Lessons: Your first system · What a request is, and p50 versus p99.

Problem: URL shortener · Practice.

Follow a request from the user to the store and back. Name the work on that path and where the response-time target applies. Finish the introduction, then attempt the shortener without looking at the editorial. Save your first bottleneck prediction.

Play this problem.

Day 2: Do the numbers

Lessons: Numbers you can do in your head · Spreading load.

Problem: URL shortener · Practice.

Repeat the shortener. Separate its normal peak from its viral event. Estimate capacity with spare room, then check whether that spare room survives losing capacity. Record the difference between your estimate and the run.

Play this problem.

Day 3: Remember repeated answers

Lessons: Remembering answers · Copies near users.

Problem: News site · Practice.

Identify which reads can share an answer and how stale it may be. Predict the effect of a cold cache before running. Keep the original data separate from copies that can be rebuilt.

Play this problem.

Day 4: Move work off the reply path

Lessons: Waiting instead of breaking · Exactly once, on purpose.

Problem: Package tracking · Practice.

Trace acceptance and completion separately. Write down the waiting deadline and the duplicate policy. Watch the age of waiting work as well as its count; a queue is only useful if work can finish in time.

Play this problem.

Day 5: Keep copies honest

Lessons: Copies are a little behind · Which copy is the truth.

Problem: Restaurant reservations · Practice.

Explain where a newly saved booking is read back and what happens if a copy is behind. Write the rule that prevents conflicting reservations, then distinguish it from the traffic capacity you measured.

Play this problem.

Day 6: Prepare for pressure

Lessons: Saying "slow down" politely · Timeouts and failing fast · Adding servers, and why it is late.

Problem: Rate limiter for a public API · Practice.

Compare refusing excess work, waiting for it and adding capacity. State the limiter outage policy. A scheduled crowd can arrive before new servers are ready, so predict the first interval separately from later recovery.

Play this problem.

Day 7: Review the first week

Lessons: Where the money goes · How to lead a design interview.

Problem: Notification service · Practice.

Do a complete attempt with a written scope, estimates and one failure prediction. Read the debrief only after recording your explanation. Write the requirement, mechanism, alternative and measurement behind one decision.

Play this problem.

Day 8: Lead the API discussion

Lessons: Many customers on one system.

Problem: Rate limiter for a public API · Interview.

Ask about per-customer fairness and shared counters before choosing a mechanism. Use the timed flow, then defend an outage policy and test one claim. Keep measured traffic results separate from written reasoning.

Open Interview mode.

Day 9: Defend delayed work

Lessons: Work across services · SLOs and error budgets.

Problem: Notification service · Interview.

Clarify urgency, provider acceptance and expiry. Explain how a lost reply differs from a confirmed failure. Defend the queue policy with observed waiting time and a tested claim about a changed workload.

Open Interview mode.

Day 10: Handle a weak connection

Lessons: Live sockets and presence · Ordering and time.

Problem: One-to-one chat · Interview.

Clarify ordering and the identity of a message across retries. Estimate message traffic separately from open connections. Explain the recovery path after a lost acknowledgement, then compare it with what the run proves.

Open Interview mode.

Day 11: Protect a booking

Lessons: Search is a copy · Copies and quorums.

Problem: Hotel booking · Interview.

Separate search results from authoritative booking state. Explain what happens when a dependency is slow or a replica is behind. Defend which work can use an old copy and which operation must wait or fail.

Open Interview mode.

Day 12: Bound fanout

Lessons: One post, millions of feeds · When one item is popular.

Problem: Social feed · Interview.

Explain how an ordinary account and a celebrity change write amplification. State the promise for your own post. Test a claim about a hot item and defend the point at which you would change the policy.

Open Interview mode.

Day 13: Design for the known rush

Lessons: Surviving a region · Seeing problems early.

Problem: Concert ticket drop · Interview.

Use the scenario’s event peak, not its quiet baseline, for admission planning. Trace a retry through seat holds and payments. Defend a failure experiment and identify the user promise that extra capacity alone cannot protect.

Open Interview mode.

Day 14: Repeat and compare

Lessons: The simplest thing that works · Designs that other teams must live with.

Problem: One-to-one chat · Interview.

Start again from the brief without loading your old design. Compare the quality of your clarification, estimates and tested claims with day ten. Keep one concrete weakness to practise next and one unnecessary part you removed.

Open Interview mode.

What to keep after two weeks

A scope and a user promise you can state before choosing services.

Estimates with units, peaks and downstream limits made explicit.

A failure trace that explains durability, ordering or duplicate handling.

An experiment with a prediction, result and reason for the next change.

A trade-off tied to a requirement and a condition that would reverse your choice.

A report is a record of one attempt. Revisit a different problem using the same mechanism, or try a New twist after passing in Practice, to check whether the idea transfers. Keep the traffic score separate from checked learning progress and from your own review of the written explanation.

# URL shortener walkthrough

By System Designer
https://systemdesigner.io/guides/url-shortener-walkthrough/

Separate durable link storage from fast redirects, estimate the read path and test what happens when a popular link outgrows its cache.

This walkthrough uses the URL shortener scenario. Try an attempt first if you want to make your own choices before reading a possible approach.

Requirements and scale

People paste a long web address and get back a short one. Millions of other people then tap that short link, so reading is almost everything. Keep every tap fast, and never lose a link.

Who uses it: 50 million people a month

Audience in plain numbers: 50,000,000 people per month

Normal peak: ≈ 5,000 requests per second

Request mix: Read: 99%; Write: 1%

Speed for 99 of 100 requests: Read: ≈ 200 ms; Write: ≈ 200 ms

Successful requests: 99.9%

Data safety: No acknowledged write may be lost.

Monthly budget: ≈ $12,000

Data at rest: ≈ 1.5 TB

Where users are: North America: 70%; Europe: 30%

Home region: North America

Waiting deadlines: Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

Short codes are 7 characters. Each stored link uses about 0.5 KB including its metadata (approx.).

About 20 new links a second on average (≈ 50 million a month, approx.).

One app server handles about 1,000 requests a second (approx.).

Estimates to work through

Reads per second at peak: ≈ 4,950 req/s. 5,000 × 0.99 (approx.)

App servers for the evening peak: ≈ 5 servers. 5,000 req/s ÷ about 1,000 per server = 5. Run at least 6, and 7 or 8 so each sits near 70 percent, and turn on autoscaling: the 3 times spike needs about 15 (approx.).

Storage after 5 years: ≈ 1.5 TB. 50 million links a month × 12 × 5 years × 0.5 KB each ≈ 1.5 TB (approx.)

Possible 7-character codes: ≈ 3,500,000,000,000 codes. 62 letters and digits, to the power of 7 ≈ 3.5 trillion, so we will not run out (approx.)

Start with the lookup, not the short code

A redirect is a lookup from a short code to a long address. Saving a link creates the durable record. Following a link should do as little work as possible. In this scenario the mapping never changes, so a previously fetched answer remains useful.

Choose how a new code becomes unique. A random code needs collision detection and a retry; a sequence is simple but guessable and needs an allocation policy. Persist the mapping before acknowledging creation. A fast redirect path cannot recover a link that was never safely stored.

A design that holds

Keep the mappings in a key-value store, which retrieves a record by its key. Put application servers behind a load balancer so no single server takes every request. A memory cache serves repeated lookups. Public, immutable redirects may also be served from edge copies close to users, reducing both origin work and travel time.

Follow both paths. A cache hit ends early. A miss reaches the authoritative mapping, then fills a copy. When many callers miss the same link, combine their fetches rather than asking the store once per caller. Collect click analytics after the redirect so a slow counter does not delay navigation.

The trade-offs

A long cache lifetime works because the mapping is immutable. That same policy would need reconsidering if links could be edited, revoked or made private. Edge copies cost money per request and introduce another policy to operate. A server-only path can be cheaper but sends more work and network travel through the origin.

What breaks it

The important test is not just warm-cache throughput. Empty the cache while a popular link is being opened. Look for the load that moves back to the store, and check whether autoscaling starts quickly enough. Keep spare capacity for the interval before new servers are ready.

Study Remembering answers and Copies near users, then try the URL shortener. Make a baseline run, change one caching decision and compare the affected path. Explain which result would make you choose the simpler server-only design.

The day that tests the design

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

19:30 · Viral spike

A post blows up. Traffic climbs to several times normal within minutes.

Traffic reaches 3 times the scheduled load; rises over 600 seconds, holds for 3,600 seconds and eases over 3,600 seconds.

12:10 · Cache stampede

The cache empties (restart, purge, mass expiry) and every request rushes to the database at once.

Recovery window: ≈ 300 seconds.

Play this problem. Keep one baseline, predict a change and compare the next full day. The in-game editorial has calibrated reference designs after you finish a traffic day.

# Rate limiter walkthrough

By System Designer
https://systemdesigner.io/guides/rate-limiter-service-walkthrough/

Build fair admission for a public API: estimate counters, choose a sharing policy and explain what happens when the limiter cannot answer.

This walkthrough uses the Rate limiter for a public API scenario. Try an attempt first if you want to make your own choices before reading a possible approach.

Requirements and scale

Developers call your public API from scripts and apps. A few misbehaving or malicious clients can crowd out everyone else. Build limits that are fair, fast and cheap, and that survive a retry storm.

Who uses it: 2 million developers

Audience in plain numbers: 2,000,000 users or devices

Normal peak: ≈ 20,000 requests per second

Request mix: Read: 85%; Write: 15%

Speed for 99 of 100 requests: Read: ≈ 250 ms; Write: ≈ 250 ms

Successful requests: 99.9%

Data safety: At most 1 minute of writes may be lost.

Monthly budget: ≈ $89,000

Data at rest: ≈ 1 TB

Where users are: North America: 60%; Europe: 40%

Home region: North America

Waiting deadlines: Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

Estimate memory for 2 million counters at about 100 bytes per key, including overhead.

Typical limit: 5,000 requests an hour per key, bursts allowed (approx.).

Estimates to work through

Writes per second at peak: ≈ 3,000 writes/s. 20,000 × 0.15

Counter memory for 2 million keys at 100 bytes each (approx.): ≈ 200 MB. 2 million keys × 100 bytes (approx.)

Limit check cost: ≈ 0.2 ms. One in-memory counter update, about the speed of a cache hit (approx.)

Decide what the limit means

A limit needs an identity, a time window and a policy for bursts. A developer key is a better starting point than an IP address when many legitimate users share a network. Decide whether the allowance is global or local to a region. That choice determines how counters must be shared.

A token bucket is one way to allow a short burst without permitting an unlimited sustained rate. Tokens accumulate up to a ceiling; a request spends one. A fixed window is easier to explain but can admit a burst on both sides of a boundary. Choose according to the promise, not the name of the algorithm.

A design that holds

Put admission before expensive application work. Filter obvious attack traffic, identify the caller, check the allowance in fast memory and pass admitted work to the service. Rejected callers need a clear response and a sensible retry time so the limiter does not create its own retry storm.

The read, decision and update of a shared counter need one atomic operation. Separate reads and writes let simultaneous requests spend the same allowance. Partition counters by caller, then examine whether one huge caller can still overload a single key.

The trade-offs

Shared counters give a more exact combined allowance but add a network dependency. Independent local counters remove that hop but multiply the total permitted traffic unless the quota is divided. Divided quotas can leave one region rejecting callers while another has spare allowance.

Choose an outage policy explicitly. Failing open keeps ordinary clients moving when the limiter fails, while exposing the service to abuse. Failing closed protects capacity but rejects legitimate work too. A limited local fallback can reduce the damage, but its allowance and reconciliation still need explaining.

What breaks it

A bot may have no useful key, a hot caller may overwhelm one counter, and clients may retry faster than useful work completes. Test those separately. Buying more application capacity does not make a per-customer policy fair or a counter update atomic.

Use Saying "slow down" politely to practise the admission rule and Many customers on one system to reason about fairness. In the Rate limiter for a public API, predict which work the limiter removes and explain the uptime cost of rejecting it.

The day that tests the design

Traffic concentrated in working hours. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

10:00 · Bot scraping

Bots try stolen passwords and scrape pages, adding unwanted traffic.

Extra attack traffic is 1 times the configured peak. Duration: ≈ 7,200 seconds.

15:30 · Retry storm

A brief failure causes clients to retry, adding load while the service recovers.

Failed calls: 90%. Duration: ≈ 30 seconds. Duration: ≈ 1,200 seconds.

Play this problem. Keep one baseline, predict a change and compare the next full day. The in-game editorial has calibrated reference designs after you finish a traffic day.

# Chat system walkthrough

By System Designer
https://systemdesigner.io/guides/chat-app-walkthrough/

Design message identity, durable acknowledgement and reconnect behavior before treating chat as a socket-count problem.

This walkthrough uses the One-to-one chat scenario. Try an attempt first if you want to make your own choices before reading a possible approach.

Requirements and scale

People send short messages to each other from their phones. A message must arrive once, in order, even when the phone is on a bad connection and sends it again. If the other person is offline, the message waits and a notification goes out.

Who uses it: 10 million people a month

Audience in plain numbers: 10,000,000 people per month

Normal peak: ≈ 20,000 requests per second

Request mix: Message: 55%; Sync change: 15%; Read: 10%; Analytics event: 10%; Sign-in: 2%; Notification: 8%

Speed for 99 of 100 requests: Message: ≈ 300 ms; Sync change: ≈ 400 ms; Read: ≈ 400 ms; Sign-in: ≈ 1,000 ms

Successful requests: 99.9%

Data safety: No acknowledged write may be lost.

Monthly budget: ≈ $60,000

Data at rest: ≈ 30 TB

Where users are: North America: 30%; Europe: 30%; Asia Pacific: 40%

Home region: North America

Waiting deadlines: Message: 900 seconds; Sync change: 900 seconds; Read: 900 seconds; Analytics event: 3,600 seconds; Sign-in: 900 seconds; Notification: 900 seconds

Fresh reads: People must see their own changes. At most 0.1% of reads may be stale in the model.

Personal reads: 95% of reads are private; a shared public copy cannot answer them.

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

A message is about 1 KB (approx.).

A delivery receipt ("delivered", "read") counts as an event.

Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

Estimates to work through

Messages per second at peak: ≈ 11,000 msg/s. 20,000 x 0.55 (approx.)

Messages stored per day: ≈ 400,000,000 messages. about 40 per person per day x 10 million (approx.)

Storage added per year: ≈ 146 TB. 400 million x 1 KB x 365 = about 146 TB (approx.)

Define one message

A phone can lose a reply after the server saved a message. When it retries, the server must recognise the same intended message. Give it a stable identity on the device before the first send. Keep that identity across reconnects and retries.

State what sent, delivered and read mean. Durable storage is a different promise from arrival on another phone. Decide where ordering applies, usually within a conversation, and how clients detect a missing sequence position after reconnecting. A timestamp by itself does not settle simultaneous events on different devices.

A design that holds

Connection gateways keep sockets open for online recipients. Chat servers validate membership, deduplicate a message and append it to durable conversation storage before acknowledging it. Store the message identity and its outcome together so a crash does not leave an unprotected gap between a duplicate check and a write.

Deliver live messages through the recipient’s connection. Use a cursor to fetch missed messages after reconnecting. Offline notifications ask the recipient to check for messages; they are a separate path with separate provider limits. A notification accepted by a provider is not proof that the phone received it.

The trade-offs

Waiting for durable copies before acknowledging adds latency but protects acknowledged messages after failure. Holding sockets consumes memory even when no message is moving. Polling is simpler in some clients but repeatedly asks the server whether anything changed.

Deduplication needs a retention policy. If its records disappear before an old client retries, a repeated message can look new. Per-conversation ordering avoids imposing a global order on unrelated conversations, but reconnect and gap repair still need a protocol.

What breaks it

Lose a gateway, then let many devices reconnect together. Check spare connection capacity, history reads and duplicate sends at the same time. Next trace a crash after storage but before acknowledgement. A smooth traffic run cannot prove that this race preserves message identity.

Work through Live sockets and presence, Exactly once, on purpose and Ordering and time. Then try One-to-one chat. Explain one recovery trace in words and one capacity failure using the measured day.

The day that tests the design

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

08:00 · Synchronized rush

Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

Traffic for Sign-in, Message, Read, Sync change reaches 10 times the scheduled load; rises over 10 seconds, holds for 60 seconds and eases over 300 seconds. Other request types keep their scheduled load.

14:00 · Zone outage

An availability zone loses power or network access.

Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

19:00 · Duplicate delivery

The queue redelivers messages. Without duplicate protection, side effects may be applied twice.

Affected share: 1%. Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

Play this problem. Keep one baseline, predict a change and compare the next full day. The in-game editorial has calibrated reference designs after you finish a traffic day.

# News feed walkthrough

By System Designer
https://systemdesigner.io/guides/social-feed-walkthrough/

Estimate fanout work, keep posts authoritative and choose where to assemble feeds for ordinary accounts and celebrities.

This walkthrough uses the Social feed scenario. Try an attempt first if you want to make your own choices before reading a possible approach.

Requirements and scale

Every person opens the app and sees a feed of posts from the people they follow. Most people have a few hundred followers, but a few have millions, and when they post, millions of feeds must change. The feed must be fast and your own post must show up at once.

Who uses it: 50 million people a month

Audience in plain numbers: 50,000,000 people per month

Normal peak: ≈ 60,000 requests per second

Request mix: Read: 80%; Analytics event: 12%; Notification: 3%; Write: 2%; Search: 2%; Sign-in: 1%

Speed for 99 of 100 requests: Read: ≈ 350 ms; Write: ≈ 350 ms; Search: ≈ 500 ms; Sign-in: ≈ 1,000 ms

Successful requests: 99.9%

Data safety: At most 1 minute of writes may be lost.

Monthly budget: ≈ $170,000

Data at rest: ≈ 60 TB

Where users are: North America: 40%; Europe: 30%; Asia Pacific: 30%

Home region: North America

Waiting deadlines: Read: 900 seconds; Analytics event: 3,600 seconds; Notification: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds; Search: 900 seconds; Sign-in: 900 seconds

Fresh reads: People must see their own changes. At most 0.1% of reads may be stale in the model.

Personal reads: 60% of reads are private; a shared public copy cannot answer them.

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

About 20 million posts are made per day (approx.).

A post is about 1 KB. Media is handled by a different system.

Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

Estimates to work through

Feed loads per second at peak: ≈ 48,000 req/s. 60,000 x 0.8 (approx.)

Posts per second on average: ≈ 230 posts/s. 20 million per day / 86,400 (approx.)

Feed updates per second with fanout on write: ≈ 46,000 writes/s. 230 posts/s x 200 followers (approx.)

Choose the unit of work

A post is one record, but it can create many feed updates. Start by separating post creation, follower delivery and reading a feed. The exercise begins with time order rather than ranking. The author must see their own post immediately; other feeds can be a few seconds behind.

Use the scenario’s Numbers values below as separate estimates with stated assumptions. Its clarification describes a rough read-to-post ratio, while its scored request mix also includes events, notifications, search and login. Use that scored mix when sizing request paths rather than treating the rough ratio as the entire workload.

A design that holds

Save the post as the source of truth. For ordinary accounts, place post identifiers into followers’ prepared feeds using queued workers. Feed reads then fetch a short list rather than scanning every followed account. Make workers restartable: a retry must not insert the same feed entry twice.

Treat very large accounts differently. Instead of writing into every follower’s feed on each celebrity post, fetch those posts when a person opens their feed and merge them with prepared entries. Include the author’s own new post directly so delayed background fanout does not hide it from its creator.

The trade-offs

Preparing feeds makes frequent reads cheap but multiplies writes by follower count. Assembling everything at read time saves those writes but moves work into the response path. A hybrid has more policy and operational complexity, so explain the measurement that justifies its threshold.

A cached feed is a shortcut, not the only copy of the post. Rebuilding it should be possible from durable posts and follow relationships. Separate private feed contents from public media that many people can share at the edge.

What breaks it

A celebrity post can grow the fanout backlog faster than workers drain it. A popular item can overload one cache partition. A cold cache can send many reads back to storage. Each is a different failure: adding shards may not split one hot key, and adding workers may only overload the destination faster.

Use One post, millions of feeds and When one item is popular before trying Social feed. Predict where work moves when you switch a large account from push to pull, then compare both write pressure and read latency.

The day that tests the design

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

12:00 · Celebrity post

A popular account posts, multiplying the work needed to update follower feeds.

Work multiplier: 25. Duration: ≈ 900 seconds.

17:30 · Hot key

One item gets a huge share of traffic: a celebrity profile, one product, one merchant.

Affected share: 30%. Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

08:15 · Cache stampede

The cache empties (restart, purge, mass expiry) and every request rushes to the database at once.

Recovery window: ≈ 300 seconds.

Play this problem. Keep one baseline, predict a change and compare the next full day. The in-game editorial has calibrated reference designs after you finish a traffic day.

# Notification service walkthrough

By System Designer
https://systemdesigner.io/guides/notification-service-walkthrough/

Separate acceptance from sending, respect provider quotas and reason about expiry and unknown outcomes before claiming delivery once.

This walkthrough uses the Notification service scenario. Try an attempt first if you want to make your own choices before reading a possible approach.

Requirements and scale

Every other team asks you to send messages: order shipped, new login, a sale starting. You send them by push, email and text through outside providers who have their own limits. Send each message once, and never block the team that asked.

Who uses it: 30 million people a month

Audience in plain numbers: 30,000,000 people per month

Normal peak: ≈ 8,000 requests per second

Request mix: Notification: 70%; Analytics event: 20%; Write: 10%

Speed for 99 of 100 requests: Write: ≈ 300 ms

Successful requests: 99.9%

Data safety: No acknowledged write may be lost.

Monthly budget: ≈ $120,000

Data at rest: ≈ 2 TB

Where users are: North America: 60%; Europe: 40%

Home region: North America

Waiting deadlines: Notification: 1,800 seconds; Analytics event: 1,800 seconds; Write: 1,800 seconds

Required proofs: Consent records

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

Providers cap how fast you may send: push ≈ 10,000/s, email ≈ 1,000/s, text ≈ 100/s (approx.).

Texts cost far more than email or push.

Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

Estimates to work through

Messages to send per second at peak: ≈ 5,600 msg/s. 8,000 × 0.7

Messages per day: ≈ 190 million. Average load is about 0.4 of peak: 5,600 × 0.4 × 86,400 ≈ 190 million (approx.)

Email sending limit: ≈ 1,000 email/s. The provider cap in this scenario: you must spread load across channels and wait politely (approx.)

Acceptance is a promise too

The caller should not wait for an email or push provider to finish. It needs to know whether work was accepted durably. Give the request an identity, check the required preference policy and record the job before returning acceptance. Decide what the caller can safely retry if the reply is lost.

Separate urgent messages from campaigns. A message that can wait through a provider outage has a different deadline from a login code. The scenario’s waiting deadline and provider-acceptance boundary below are the promises to test; they do not prove device receipt.

A design that holds

Use durable queues to decouple callers from sending. Workers consume at a pace each provider allows, recheck preferences, track attempts and preserve the same logical key across retries. Keep an explicit state for work whose provider outcome is unknown.

A local duplicate lookup alone cannot guarantee one external send after a crash. If a provider accepted the message but the worker died before recording that fact, a retry needs the provider’s idempotency support or a reconciliation path. State that dependency instead of claiming a queue solves it.

Separate channels or urgency classes so one throttled provider cannot block everything. Quarantine permanently bad work with a dead-letter policy, meaning a place for failed jobs that need inspection rather than endless retries. Track oldest waiting age and terminal outcomes, not only queue length.

The trade-offs

Buffering absorbs bursts but spends the delivery deadline. More workers only help while the destination has capacity. More providers add resilience but also quotas, costs and an ambiguous handover point where both may send the same message.

Texts have a much smaller quota and a different bill from push or email in this scenario. Do not split traffic equally across channels without checking those limits. A cheap default channel is useful only if it meets the message’s product requirements.

What breaks it

Throttle a provider and keep accepting new work. Ask whether spare sending capacity can clear the backlog before the oldest jobs expire. Next make one message fail repeatedly and check that urgent work still progresses. Finally trace a lost provider reply and explain how the next worker discovers the outcome.

Use Waiting instead of breaking and Work across services, then try Notification service. Defend the difference between a fast acceptance response and a completed send using both the run and a crash trace.

The day that tests the design

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

09:00 · Provider rate limit

An outside service lowers its configured request quota and answers 'too many requests' above the reduced limit.

Provider capacity falls to 40% of its configured quota. Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

13:00 · Duplicate delivery

The queue redelivers messages. Without duplicate protection, side effects may be applied twice.

Affected share: 3%. Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

18:30 · Dependency outage

An outside service fails calls during an outage.

Failed calls: 100%. Duration: ≈ 1,200 seconds.

Play this problem. Keep one baseline, predict a change and compare the next full day. The in-game editorial has calibrated reference designs after you finish a traffic day.

# Caching, load balancing and queues, explained by breaking things

By System Designer
https://systemdesigner.io/guides/caching-load-balancing-queues/

Three small experiments show what caching, load balancing and queues protect, what they cost and how each can fail.

These parts solve different problems. A load balancer shares work, a cache avoids repeated work and a queue postpones work. They often appear together, but adding all three without an explanation makes a failure harder to understand.

Experiment: spread the same work

Open Spreading load. Before touching the controls, predict what happens when several servers exist but clients still send requests to one address. Extra capacity only helps if requests can reach it.

A load balancer selects a healthy server for each request. Remove one server and ask whether the remaining pool has enough room. Spreading work does not create capacity, and health routing does not make a slow database faster. Watch the whole path rather than stopping at the front-end pool.

Compare an even rotation with choosing the least busy server when requests take different lengths of time. Then consider held-open connections: moving new requests is easier than moving an existing conversation. State which load the balancing policy actually sees.

Experiment: avoid repeated work

Open Remembering answers. Its database is nearly full and repeated answers may be at most 60 seconds old. Put a cache on the request path and predict how many reads still reach the database. The lesson’s check questions ask how hit rate changes that work; remember that writes still need their own path.

A time to live, or TTL, bounds how long an answer may remain in that cache without refresh. More memory does not make an old answer fresh. Long-lived copies help stable public data, while balances or private responses need a different policy.

Now use the URL shortener to test a cache stampede. When a copy empties, simultaneous misses can repeat the original work. Combining identical fetches limits that rush; spare storage capacity still matters for unrelated misses.

Experiment: spend time instead of dropping work

Open Waiting instead of breaking. Work enters a queue before workers send it to the destination. Predict whether the backlog grows by comparing arrival and completion rates. Only completion capacity above new arrivals is available to drain old work.

A queue can make a short burst survivable, but it cannot make an indefinitely overloaded destination keep up. Watch the oldest waiting job against its deadline. A smaller queue with very old work can be worse for users than a larger queue that drains quickly.

Try the Notification service next. Its providers have quotas. Increasing worker count beyond a quota adds contention or retries, not successful sends. Admission control tells callers when work cannot be accepted safely; backpressure slows producers when downstream work is already full.

Combine them by following one request

Say which step returns a reply. A cache hit may end before the application reaches storage. An accepted queued job may return before its external effect happens. A load balancer chooses a server, but that server still waits for its dependencies.

For balancing, measure healthy capacity and the work left after one unit fails.

For caching, measure hit rate, freshness and load while copies are cold.

For queues, measure arrivals, drain rate, oldest age and the deadline.

For all three, compare the monthly cost with the promise they protect.

Keep the workload fixed when comparing designs. Change one policy at a time and say what result would disprove your explanation. That habit is more useful than remembering where these boxes usually sit in a reference diagram.

## Problem catalogue

### URL shortener
https://systemdesigner.io/p/url-shortener/
Easy; Core building blocks.
People paste a long web address and get back a short one. Millions of other people then tap that short link, so reading is almost everything. Keep every tap fast, and never lose a link.
Audience: 50 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 5000 requests/s; budget ≈ $12000/month.
Concepts: Remembering answers, Numbers you can do in your head, Consistent hashing and moving data, The simplest thing that works, How to lead a design interview.

### Rate limiter for a public API
https://systemdesigner.io/p/rate-limiter-service/
Medium; Core building blocks.
Developers call your public API from scripts and apps. A few misbehaving or malicious clients can crowd out everyone else. Build limits that are fair, fast and cheap, and that survive a retry storm.
Audience: 2 million developers; normal peak ≈ 20000 requests/s; budget ≈ $89000/month.
Concepts: Saying "slow down" politely, When one item is popular, Many customers on one system, Agreeing on one leader.

### Search autocomplete
https://systemdesigner.io/p/search-autocomplete/
Medium; Core building blocks.
As people type, they expect suggestions after every letter, in the blink of an eye. Most people type the same popular beginnings. When news breaks, one phrase suddenly dominates.
Audience: 200 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 60000 requests/s; budget ≈ $92000/month.
Concepts: Remembering answers, Search is a copy.

### Notification service
https://systemdesigner.io/p/notification-service/
Medium; Core building blocks.
Every other team asks you to send messages: order shipped, new login, a sale starting. You send them by push, email and text through outside providers who have their own limits. Send each message once, and never block the team that asked.
Audience: 30 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 8000 requests/s; budget ≈ $120000/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Exactly once, on purpose, Work across services, SLOs and error budgets, Designs that other teams must live with.

### Login and single sign-on
https://systemdesigner.io/p/login-sso/
Medium; Core building blocks.
Employees and customers sign in to many apps through one account. Most of the day is quiet, then 9 am arrives and everyone signs in at once. Attackers also hammer the login with stolen passwords. Let real people in quickly and keep the rest out.
Audience: 8 million people a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 6000 requests/s; budget ≈ $63000/month.
Concepts: Saying "slow down" politely, Proof built in.

### Scheduled job service
https://systemdesigner.io/p/job-scheduler/
Hard; Core building blocks.
Customers register jobs: "call my web address every night at 02:00" or "every hour on the hour". Aim to fire within 5 seconds; work still waiting after 60 seconds counts as failed. Retry safely after a crash. One external effect requires the customer endpoint to honor a stable job occurrence key. Half the world picks the top of the hour, so a huge crowd of jobs comes due in the same second.
Audience: 300,000 customers and 40 million jobs (approx.); normal peak ≈ 1200 requests/s; budget ≈ $7700/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Exactly once, on purpose, Agreeing on one leader, Work across services, Ordering and time.

### Object storage service
https://systemdesigner.io/p/object-storage/
Hard; Core building blocks.
Customers store billions of files, from tiny pictures to huge videos, and fetch them by name. The service must never lose a file, scale without a limit and stay cheap. Most files are written once and rarely read again.
Audience: 5 million developers and apps (approx.); normal peak ≈ 12000 requests/s; budget ≈ $170000/month.
Concepts: Hot, warm, cold and archive, Splitting data, Consistent hashing and moving data, Copies and quorums, Inside a storage engine.

### Photo sharing
https://systemdesigner.io/p/photo-sharing/
Easy; Media and streaming.
You are building a photo app. People post pictures and everyone else scrolls through them. Almost all the traffic is people looking at photos, and the photos take up far more room than anything else you store.
Audience: 30 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 6000 requests/s; budget ≈ $24000/month.
Concepts: Copies near users, Hot, warm, cold and archive.

### Podcast hosting
https://systemdesigner.io/p/podcast-hosting/
Easy; Media and streaming.
You host shows for creators. Listeners press play and download big audio files, and creators upload a new episode now and then. The audio is the bill: every episode downloaded costs bandwidth.
Audience: 200 thousand listeners a month; normal peak ≈ 40 requests/s; budget ≈ $7700/month.
Concepts: Copies near users, Where the money goes.

### News site
https://systemdesigner.io/p/news-site/
Easy; Media and streaming.
You run a news site. Millions read the same few stories, and when something big happens almost everyone opens the same page in the same minute. Editors publish all day, and readers expect fresh headlines.
Audience: 20 million readers a month; normal peak ≈ 8000 requests/s; budget ≈ $44000/month.
Concepts: Remembering answers, Copies near users.

### Music streaming
https://systemdesigner.io/p/music-streaming/
Medium; Media and streaming.
People search for songs, build playlists and press play. The audio is the heavy part, and a hit song is played by millions at once. Playback must not stutter, even when part of your system fails.
Audience: 1.5 million listeners a month; normal peak ≈ 500 requests/s; budget ≈ $46000/month.
Concepts: Copies near users, Remembering answers, Search is a copy.

### Video streaming
https://systemdesigner.io/p/video-on-demand/
Medium; Media and streaming.
You run a movie and series service for a growing audience. Each viewer pulls a few seconds of video at a time for two hours straight. Bandwidth is the largest cost by far, and everyone wants to start watching in the evening.
Audience: 400 thousand subscribers; normal peak ≈ 600 requests/s; budget ≈ $108000/month.
Concepts: Copies near users, Where the money goes, Hot, warm, cold and archive.

### Short-video feed
https://systemdesigner.io/p/short-video-feed/
Medium; Media and streaming.
People swipe through an endless feed of clips of 10 to 30 seconds. The next clip must already be on the phone before the swipe. One clip can suddenly get millions of views, and every view is a signal that picks what to show next.
Audience: 2 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 1500 requests/s; budget ≈ $170000/month.
Concepts: Copies near users, Remembering answers, When one item is popular.

### Video upload pipeline
https://systemdesigner.io/p/video-upload-pipeline/
Hard; Media and streaming.
Creators upload videos that must be converted into several qualities before anyone can watch. Conversion is slow, costs real money per video, and the converter sometimes fails on a broken file. Nothing a creator uploads can be lost.
Audience: 8 million viewers a month, 15 thousand uploads a day; normal peak ≈ 150 requests/s; budget ≈ $740000/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Exactly once, on purpose.

### Live streaming
https://systemdesigner.io/p/live-streaming/
Hard; Media and streaming.
Streamers broadcast live and thousands watch together, with a chat on the side. Everyone wants the same piece of video at the same second, so nothing can be saved for later. When a big streamer goes live, the whole audience arrives at once.
Audience: 1 million viewers a month, thousands live at once; normal peak ≈ 3200 requests/s; budget ≈ $270000/month.
Concepts: Copies near users, Live sockets and presence, One post, millions of feeds.

### Comments and likes
https://systemdesigner.io/p/comments-and-likes/
Easy; Social and messaging.
Under every post sits a like counter and a comment list. Millions tap the heart on the same famous post at the same moment. Showing the exact number is not essential, but showing the person their own like is.
Audience: 10 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 30000 requests/s; budget ≈ $94000/month.
Concepts: When one item is popular, Remembering answers.

### One-to-one chat
https://systemdesigner.io/p/chat-app/
Medium; Social and messaging.
People send short messages to each other from their phones. A message must arrive once, in order, even when the phone is on a bad connection and sends it again. If the other person is offline, the message waits and a notification goes out.
Audience: 10 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 20000 requests/s; budget ≈ $60000/month.
Concepts: Live sockets and presence, Exactly once, on purpose, Ordering and time, What consistent really means, Syncing across devices.

### Disappearing stories
https://systemdesigner.io/p/stories/
Medium; Social and messaging.
People post photos and short clips that vanish after 24 hours. Followers tap through a tray of stories every day, and the poster sees who looked. Deleting on time matters: storage must not grow forever.
Audience: 5 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 3000 requests/s; budget ≈ $78000/month.
Concepts: Hot, warm, cold and archive, Copies near users.

### Social feed
https://systemdesigner.io/p/social-feed/
Hard; Social and messaging.
Every person opens the app and sees a feed of posts from the people they follow. Most people have a few hundred followers, but a few have millions, and when they post, millions of feeds must change. The feed must be fast and your own post must show up at once.
Audience: 50 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 60000 requests/s; budget ≈ $170000/month.
Concepts: One post, millions of feeds, Remembering answers, When one item is popular.

### Group chat and presence
https://systemdesigner.io/p/group-chat-presence/
Hard; Social and messaging.
Teams talk in channels with many people. Everyone sees messages in the same order, sees who is online and who is typing, and gets notified when mentioned. At nine every morning thousands of workplaces start at once, and one announcement can reach a channel of tens of thousands.
Audience: 3 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 25000 requests/s; budget ≈ $74000/month.
Concepts: Live sockets and presence, One post, millions of feeds, Which copy is the truth.

### Invoicing and billing
https://systemdesigner.io/p/invoicing-billing/
Easy; Finance and payments.
Small businesses create invoices, email them to customers and take card payments online. On the last working day of the month everyone sends and chases invoices at once. Nobody may get the same invoice email twice, and no invoice may vanish.
Audience: 300,000 small businesses and their customers; normal peak ≈ 800 requests/s; budget ≈ $5500/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Exactly once, on purpose.

### Payroll run
https://systemdesigner.io/p/payroll-run/
Easy; Finance and payments.
On pay day your system tells the payment rail to move salaries for two million employees, then publishes a payslip for each one. Employees open the app at breakfast to see if they were paid. Paying anyone twice is the one thing you must never do.
Audience: 2 million employees at 40,000 companies; normal peak ≈ 2400 requests/s; budget ≈ $8600/month.
Concepts: Exactly once, on purpose, Waiting instead of breaking.

### Checkout payments
https://systemdesigner.io/p/payments-checkout/
Medium; Finance and payments.
Online shops send you their customers at the moment they pay. You call a card processor, record the order and answer in a couple of seconds. When the processor is slow or down, shoppers refresh and tap Pay again.
Audience: 8 million shoppers a month; normal peak ≈ 2000 requests/s; budget ≈ $5200/month.
Concepts: Exactly once, on purpose, Timeouts and failing fast, Work across services, What consistent really means.

### Peer-to-peer wallet
https://systemdesigner.io/p/digital-wallet/
Medium; Finance and payments.
People split dinner by sending each other money from their phones. A transfer takes money from one balance and adds it to another, and the sender must see the new balance right away. A flaky mobile connection often makes the app send the same transfer twice.
Audience: 600,000 active people a month; normal peak ≈ 2500 requests/s; budget ≈ $9800/month.
Concepts: Which copy is the truth, Exactly once, on purpose, Proof built in.

### Insurance claims
https://systemdesigner.io/p/insurance-claims/
Medium; Finance and payments.
After a hailstorm, thousands of drivers file claims online, each with a handful of photos. The storm offer ends at 5 pm, so everyone files at the last minute. Every claim must be saved safely, and every customer gets a confirmation email.
Audience: 3 million policyholders; normal peak ≈ 400 requests/s; budget ≈ $14000/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Proof built in.

### Buy now, pay later
https://systemdesigner.io/p/bnpl-credit/
Medium; Finance and payments.
At checkout a shopper picks "pay in four". You score the shopper in a few seconds, then charge the first quarter on their card. The card network sometimes asks you to slow down, and when apps retry, the retries make it worse.
Audience: 2 million shoppers a month; normal peak ≈ 3000 requests/s; budget ≈ $8700/month.
Concepts: Timeouts and failing fast, Waiting instead of breaking, Exactly once, on purpose.

### Bank ledger
https://systemdesigner.io/p/bank-ledger/
Hard; Finance and payments.
You run the system of record for a regional bank: every deposit, withdrawal and card settlement is a posting that must be exact and permanent. Customers in two continents read balances all day, and regulators can ask for proof at any time. A bad day for you is a loss of even one posting.
Audience: 400,000 customers; normal peak ≈ 6000 requests/s; budget ≈ $33000/month.
Concepts: Which copy is the truth, Proof built in, Surviving a region, Copies and quorums, What consistent really means, Inside a storage engine.

### Stock order matching
https://systemdesigner.io/p/stock-order-matching/
Hard; Finance and payments.
Brokers and traders send buy and sell orders, and you pair them fairly: the earliest order at the best price goes first. At the market open a rush of orders arrives in seconds. Every accepted order must be in one agreed sequence, and no trade may be lost or invented.
Audience: 300,000 active traders and 300 broker systems; normal peak ≈ 10000 requests/s; budget ≈ $35000/month.
Concepts: Which copy is the truth, Waiting instead of breaking.

### Real-time fraud detection
https://systemdesigner.io/p/fraud-detection/
Hard; Finance and payments.
Every card payment asks your system "is this fraud?" and wants the answer within about 150 milliseconds. Each check looks up the cardholder's recent habits and runs a model. The holiday shopping rush doubles the volume, and a bad model update can start declining honest customers.
Audience: 20 million cardholders; normal peak ≈ 5000 requests/s; budget ≈ $22000/month.
Concepts: GPUs, tokens and fallbacks, Timeouts and failing fast.

### Crypto exchange
https://systemdesigner.io/p/crypto-exchange/
Hard; Finance and payments.
People trade coins, check prices and withdraw funds around the clock from every continent. A sudden price crash makes everyone log in and trade at once, attackers flood you hoping to knock the site over, and a leaked key could empty a wallet. Balances must never be wrong.
Audience: 3 million traders, 300,000 active in a month; normal peak ≈ 6000 requests/s; budget ≈ $32000/month.
Concepts: Saying "slow down" politely, Which copy is the truth, Proof built in.

### Clinic appointment booking
https://systemdesigner.io/p/appointment-booking/
Easy; Healthcare.
A group of 60 clinics lets patients find a free slot, book it and get a text reminder. Slots open at 8 am, and the phone lines used to melt. Two people must never get the same slot, and reminders must go out even when the text-message company has a bad hour.
Audience: 300 thousand patients a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 300 requests/s; budget ≈ $7600/month.
Concepts: Which copy is the truth, Waiting instead of breaking.

### Lab results portal
https://systemdesigner.io/p/lab-results/
Easy; Healthcare.
Labs send results to a portal, patients get a notice that a result is ready and open it. When the notice goes to thousands of people at the same minute, they all open the portal at once. Nobody should get the same notice twice.
Audience: 1.2 million patients a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 700 requests/s; budget ≈ $12000/month.
Concepts: Remembering answers, Waiting instead of breaking, Exactly once, on purpose, Privacy by design, Work across services.

### Patient health records
https://systemdesigner.io/p/health-records/
Medium; Healthcare.
A hospital network keeps patient charts, orders, notes and scanned documents for 40 hospitals. Doctors need a chart in under a second, no saved note may be lost when a server or a building fails (in a whole-region disaster, at most the last minute of edits may need re-entering from the ward), and an auditor can walk in any day and ask you to prove who looked at what.
Audience: 25,000 staff, 3 million patients (approx.); normal peak ≈ 3000 requests/s; budget ≈ $52000/month.
Concepts: Proof built in, Surviving a region, Privacy by design, Changing a running system, Designs that other teams must live with.

### Telehealth video visits
https://systemdesigner.io/p/telehealth-video/
Medium; Healthcare.
Patients join a video visit with a doctor from their phone. Most calls go straight between the two people, but the platform runs the waiting room, chat, sign-in, the join link and a relay for the calls that cannot connect directly. A bad minute here means a patient staring at a spinner.
Audience: 800,000 visits a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 3000 requests/s; budget ≈ $24000/month.
Concepts: Live sockets and presence, Surviving a region.

### Pharmacy stock and refills
https://systemdesigner.io/p/pharmacy-stock/
Medium; Healthcare.
A pharmacy chain with 4,000 stores tracks how many boxes of each medicine every store has, takes refill requests, and shows patients which nearby store has their medicine today. If the system says a store has a box that is gone, a patient makes a wasted trip.
Audience: 9 million patients, 4,000 stores (approx.); normal peak ≈ 2500 requests/s; budget ≈ $130000/month.
Concepts: Copies are a little behind, Search is a copy.

### Vaccine sign-up surge
https://systemdesigner.io/p/vaccine-signup-surge/
Hard; Healthcare.
A county opens 80,000 vaccine appointments at 8 am. Within seconds, thousands of people reload and bots try to grab slots. The site must stay up, never sell the same slot twice, and be fair to people on a phone with a poor signal.
Audience: 4 million residents; 600,000 try on launch day (approx.); normal peak ≈ 300 requests/s; budget ≈ $58000/month.
Concepts: Saying "slow down" politely, Waiting instead of breaking.

### Health readings from a wearable
https://systemdesigner.io/p/wearable-health/
Hard; Healthcare.
A wearable records health readings even when its phone or cloud service is unavailable. Keep raw readings on the device when possible and upload only consented summaries in sparse batches. The system must not lose locally saved readings during a supported outage, and deleting an account must have a verifiable end-to-end workflow.
Audience: 100,000 wearables with sparse opt-in uploads (approx.); normal peak ≈ 500 requests/s; budget ≈ $2100/month.
Concepts: Privacy by design, Syncing across devices, Inside a storage engine, Ordering and time, SLOs and error budgets.

### Benefits application portal
https://systemdesigner.io/p/benefits-portal/
Easy; Government and education.
People apply for food, health or housing help on a state site. Forms are long, people save drafts and upload documents, and a caseworker team reviews each one. The last week of the month is busy, and an auditor checks the privacy and access controls once a year.
Audience: 1.5 million applicants a year (approx.); normal peak ≈ 300 requests/s; budget ≈ $8500/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Proof built in.

### Course enrollment day
https://systemdesigner.io/p/course-enrollment-day/
Medium; Government and education.
Registration opens at 9 am for 40,000 students, and a handful of popular courses have only 30 seats each. Everyone clicks "enroll" at the same moment, and when the page is slow they click again. A seat must go to exactly one student.
Audience: 40,000 students, 12 courses each (approx.); normal peak ≈ 4000 requests/s; budget ≈ $38000/month.
Concepts: When one item is popular, Saying "slow down" politely.

### Online exam
https://systemdesigner.io/p/online-exam/
Medium; Government and education.
A national board runs a two-hour online exam for 200,000 students in three regions at the same time. Answers save automatically every half minute, a live heartbeat shows the student is still there, and proctoring marks suspicious events. Every saved answer matters. A minute of outage at the wrong time is a national story.
Audience: 200,000 students at the same time (approx.); normal peak ≈ 25000 requests/s; budget ≈ $49000/month.
Concepts: Live sockets and presence, Surviving a region.

### Tax filing deadline
https://systemdesigner.io/p/tax-deadline-surge/
Hard; Government and education.
A national tax site lets 30 million people file online. Most wait until deadline day, and traffic climbs all evening to a final-hour rush. People upload forms, check what they owe and pay. A mistake in a payment or a leak of tax data is a national story.
Audience: 30 million filers over the season (approx.); normal peak ≈ 8000 requests/s; budget ≈ $260000/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Adding servers, and why it is late, Proof built in.

### Package tracking
https://systemdesigner.io/p/package-tracking/
Easy; Mobility and logistics.
You run the tracking page for a parcel company. People refresh it again and again while they wait for a delivery, and depots send a scan every time a parcel moves. Keep the page fast, lose at most the last minute of scans in a failure (scanners keep a copy and can resend), and make sure a broken text-message service cannot slow anything down.
Audience: 20 million people a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 3000 requests/s; budget ≈ $16000/month.
Concepts: Remembering answers, Waiting instead of breaking.

### Fleet telemetry
https://systemdesigner.io/p/fleet-telemetry/
Medium; Mobility and logistics.
A freight company has 150,000 trucks that each send a batch of sensor readings every 30 seconds. Dispatchers watch live maps and analysts run reports. You must take in every batch, keep a month of detail cheaply, and survive the moments when thousands of trucks come back online at once.
Audience: 150,000 trucks and 3,000 dispatchers and analysts (approx.); normal peak ≈ 6000 requests/s; budget ≈ $9700/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Hot, warm, cold and archive, Seeing problems early, How metrics systems work, Inside a storage engine.

### Food delivery
https://systemdesigner.io/p/food-delivery/
Medium; Mobility and logistics.
You run food delivery in a few big cities. People browse menus, pay for an order, and watch a courier move on a map. Dinner time is brutal, and the payment company sometimes slows down. Nobody may be charged twice, and no paid order may vanish.
Audience: 8 million people a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 5000 requests/s; budget ≈ $15000/month.
Concepts: Live sockets and presence, Exactly once, on purpose, Timeouts and failing fast.

### Ride-hailing dispatch
https://systemdesigner.io/p/ride-hailing-dispatch/
Hard; Mobility and logistics.
You run dispatch for a big metro area. About 100,000 drivers send a position every 4 seconds, and riders ask for cars near them. When a stadium empties, thousands of riders ask for a car from the same few blocks at the same moment. Match riders to drivers fast, and never charge a trip twice.
Audience: 15 million riders and 600,000 drivers a month, 100,000 drivers online at peak (approx.); normal peak ≈ 30000 requests/s; budget ≈ $40000/month.
Concepts: Live sockets and presence, When one item is popular, Splitting data.

### Maps and routing
https://systemdesigner.io/p/maps-routing/
Hard; Mobility and logistics.
You run a maps app with places, routes and live traffic. Map pictures never change much, but route lookups, place search and traffic from moving phones do. Soon a whole new continent will start using it. Keep maps fast everywhere without paying to serve the same picture twice.
Audience: 20 million people a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 12000 requests/s; budget ≈ $41000/month.
Concepts: Copies near users, Remembering answers, Surviving a region.

### Restaurant reservations
https://systemdesigner.io/p/restaurant-reservations/
Easy; Travel and events.
Diners look up restaurants, check which tables are free tonight and book one. Looking is easy to speed up. Booking is not: two people must never get the same table. Friday at 5 pm is the busy moment.
Audience: 6 million diners a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 1500 requests/s; budget ≈ $2500/month.
Concepts: Which copy is the truth, Remembering answers.

### Hotel booking
https://systemdesigner.io/p/hotel-booking/
Medium; Travel and events.
You run a hotel booking site. People search for rooms, open hotel pages and book. Search can be a little behind, but you must never sell the last room twice. Bots copy your prices all day, and sometimes the payment company slows down.
Audience: 30 million people a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 8000 requests/s; budget ≈ $12000/month.
Concepts: Search is a copy, Which copy is the truth, Saying "slow down" politely.

### Airline booking
https://systemdesigner.io/p/airline-booking/
Hard; Travel and events.
You run the booking system for an airline. Fare searches are heavy, seats are limited, and every flight needs the right number of tickets, no more and no fewer. You depend on a partner system for fares from other airlines, and it has strict limits. A fare sale and a slow partner will both happen on the same day.
Audience: 20 million visitors a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 6000 requests/s; budget ≈ $53000/month.
Concepts: Which copy is the truth, Timeouts and failing fast, Proof built in.

### Concert ticket drop
https://systemdesigner.io/p/concert-ticket-drop/
Hard; Travel and events.
Tickets for a huge tour go on sale at 10:00 sharp. Hundreds of thousands of fans arrive in the same minute, bots arrive earlier, and everyone refreshes when the page stalls. There are 40,000 seats. Sell each one once, charge each buyer once, and keep the site standing.
Audience: 2 million fans on the day (approx.); normal peak ≈ 600 requests/s; budget ≈ $16000/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Saying "slow down" politely, Exactly once, on purpose, Agreeing on one leader, What consistent really means.

### EV charging network
https://systemdesigner.io/p/ev-charging-network/
Easy; IoT and devices.
Thousands of chargers report their status every few seconds and send a record when a session ends. Drivers open an app to find a free charger. A session record must never be lost or counted twice, because it becomes a bill.
Audience: 2 million drivers a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 1800 requests/s; budget ≈ $4500/month.
Concepts: Exactly once, on purpose, Waiting instead of breaking.

### Smart home
https://systemdesigner.io/p/smart-home-hub/
Medium; IoT and devices.
One million homes have a hub that keeps a live connection to your cloud. The hub reports its devices every few minutes, and the phone app sends commands like "lock the door". Commands must feel instant and must not be repeated. Once in a while a power cut ends and every hub reconnects together.
Audience: 1 million homes and 2.5 million app users (approx.); normal peak ≈ 5000 requests/s; budget ≈ $20000/month.
Concepts: Live sockets and presence, Surviving a region, Waiting instead of breaking, Syncing across devices, Privacy by design.

### Smart power grid
https://systemdesigner.io/p/smart-power-grid/
Medium; IoT and devices.
A power company has 5 million smart meters. Each reports usage every 15 minutes, and they all try on the quarter hour. Customers see their usage, billing needs exact totals for seven years, and a regulator checks that records are kept safely. Control commands to home batteries and thermostats must never run twice.
Audience: 5 million meters, 3 million customers who look at usage (approx.); normal peak ≈ 7000 requests/s; budget ≈ $18000/month.
Concepts: Hot, warm, cold and archive, Waiting instead of breaking, Proof built in.

### Factory sensors
https://systemdesigner.io/p/industrial-sensors/
Medium; IoT and devices.
A factory has thousands of machines, each sending readings many times a second. Engineers open charts of the last hour and last month, and an alarm must fire within seconds when a reading goes out of range. The data grows without end.
Audience: 10,000 sensors and 300 engineers (approx.); normal peak ≈ 3000 requests/s; budget ≈ $9000/month.
Concepts: Hot, warm, cold and archive, Seeing problems early, Inside a storage engine, Ordering and time, How metrics systems work.

### Firmware rollout
https://systemdesigner.io/p/firmware-rollout/
Hard; IoT and devices.
A new firmware goes out to a million smart devices at 03:00 when they are idle. Every device asks "is there an update?", then downloads the same file in pieces, then reports back. If they all wake together, they can flatten your service, and a device that fails to update must not be left broken.
Audience: 1 million devices (approx.); normal peak ≈ 600 requests/s; budget ≈ $4900/month.
Concepts: Copies near users, Saying "slow down" politely.

### Semantic search
https://systemdesigner.io/p/semantic-search/
Easy; AI, ads and search.
A help center lets people type a question in plain words and finds the right articles even when the words differ. Each question is turned into a list of numbers (a vector) and matched to similar articles. Many people ask the same few questions.
Audience: 3 million people a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 400 requests/s; budget ≈ $2800/month.
Concepts: GPUs, tokens and fallbacks, Search is a copy.

### Recommendations
https://systemdesigner.io/p/recommendations/
Medium; AI, ads and search.
Every page shows a row of things the visitor might like. A ranking model builds each row, but the model is slow and costly. The row must appear instantly, even when the model is having a bad day.
Audience: 20 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 15000 requests/s; budget ≈ $19000/month.
Concepts: Remembering answers, GPUs, tokens and fallbacks.

### Ad serving
https://systemdesigner.io/p/ad-serving/
Hard; AI, ads and search.
Each page view asks you to pick the best ad in about a quarter of a second: check who is allowed to see what, score the candidates with a model, run a quick auction and answer. Every impression and click must be counted exactly because money depends on it.
Audience: 60 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 50000 requests/s; budget ≈ $140000/month.
Concepts: Remembering answers, Where the money goes, GPUs, tokens and fallbacks.

### AI chatbot serving
https://systemdesigner.io/p/ai-chatbot-serving/
Hard; AI, ads and search.
Millions of people ask your assistant questions. Each reply takes a GPU several seconds, and GPUs are expensive and sometimes simply unavailable. Keep replies flowing, protect your wallet from abuse, and have a plan for when the GPUs run out.
Audience: 8 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 800 requests/s; budget ≈ $130000/month.
Concepts: GPUs, tokens and fallbacks, Where the money goes, Saying "slow down" politely.

### Leaderboards
https://systemdesigner.io/p/leaderboards/
Easy; Games.
Players send their score at the end of every match and open the top-100 table all day. Everyone looks at the same top 100, which makes that one answer extremely popular. A tournament final will make it much worse.
Audience: 8 million players a month; normal peak ≈ 6000 requests/s; budget ≈ $20000/month.
Concepts: When one item is popular, Remembering answers.

### Multiplayer matchmaking
https://systemdesigner.io/p/matchmaking/
Medium; Games.
Players press Play and wait. You must put them in a match with others nearby, with similar skill, in a few seconds. Players in a far-away region will have a bad time, so you must keep each region close.
Audience: 3 million players online at peak; normal peak ≈ 12000 requests/s; budget ≈ $32000/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Surviving a region.

### Patch day downloads
https://systemdesigner.io/p/game-patch-day/
Medium; Games.
A popular game ships a 5 GB update at 10 am. Millions of players press Update within the same hour. The files are identical for everyone, so the work is moving huge amounts of data without a huge bill, while players still log in and play.
Audience: 12 million players a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 120 requests/s; budget ≈ $34000/month.
Concepts: Copies near users, Where the money goes.

### Battle royale launch
https://systemdesigner.io/p/battle-royale/
Hard; Games.
On launch night millions of players queue for matches of 100. Each match streams positions many times a second, the lobby shows the live player count, and one patch notes page is opened by everyone. Connections must stay open, a match server dying must preserve acknowledged progress within the stated recovery point, and a few hot items, like the daily reward, are hit by everybody.
Audience: 5 million players a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 15000 requests/s; budget ≈ $16000/month.
Concepts: Live sockets and presence, When one item is popular.

### Calendar and invites
https://systemdesigner.io/p/calendar-invites/
Easy; Productivity.
People view their week, create meetings and invite others. Each invite sends an email or phone alert. Monday at 9 am everyone opens the calendar at once. A repeated send must never produce two invites, and a slow email partner must not slow the calendar.
Audience: 10 million people a month (approx.); normal peak ≈ 1200 requests/s; budget ≈ $7100/month.
Concepts: Waiting instead of breaking, Exactly once, on purpose.

### File sync
https://systemdesigner.io/p/file-sync/
Medium; Productivity.
A folder on your laptop mirrors to the cloud and to your other devices. Small changes must arrive quickly, big files must upload reliably, and a shared folder with thousands of people must not melt the metadata service.
Audience: 3 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 4000 requests/s; budget ≈ $54000/month.
Concepts: Hot, warm, cold and archive, Which copy is the truth, Syncing across devices, Privacy by design, Consistent hashing and moving data.

### Collaborative documents
https://systemdesigner.io/p/collaborative-docs/
Hard; Productivity.
Many people edit the same document at the same moment and everyone must see a consistent result in a fraction of a second. Edits must never be lost, even if a server crashes in the middle of typing or two people type in the same place.
Audience: 15 million people a month; normal peak ≈ 40000 requests/s; budget ≈ $83000/month.
Concepts: Live sockets and presence, Which copy is the truth, Agreeing on one leader, Ordering and time, Syncing across devices.

### Email service
https://systemdesigner.io/p/email-service/
Hard; Productivity.
